nodes.description: Resorption fails while formation continues, so dense, poorly remodelled, mechanically brittle bone accumulates. Osteoclasts remain present and are not reduced in number - this is an osteoclast-rich osteopetrosis, the category shared with TCIRG1, CLCN7, OSTM1 and SNX10 disease and distinct from the osteoclast-poor RANKL/RANK forms, in which osteoclasts fail to be generated at all. The practical consequence is that supplying normal osteoclast precursors can rescue this arm, which is why transplantation works on the bone and on nothing else.

nodes.description: Transplantation supplies CA II-competent osteoclast precursors, which are hematopoietic in origin, and can resolve the osteopetrosis histologically and radiologically. It is an arm-specific therapy by construction: the renal tubule and the brain are not hematopoietic, keep their own enzyme defect, and are unaffected. Reported indications have been severe progressive visual and hearing loss rather than marrow failure. This is emphatically not the default management of CA2 deficiency the way it is for TCIRG1 malignant infantile osteopetrosis: this is an intermediate osteopetrosis whose skeletal phenotype often improves with age and which is compatible with a normal lifespan, so transplantation is reserved.

nodes.description: Both CA2 alleles carry loss-of-function variants - splice-junction, nonsense, frameshift or missense - and carbonic anhydrase II protein is absent or catalytically dead in every tissue that normally expresses it. The erythrocyte is the accessible readout: the isoenzyme II peak, its esterase and CO2 hydratase activities, and immunoprecipitable enzyme are all essentially absent, while CA I is spared. Reported mechanisms of loss include abolished splicing (the intron 2 founder allele), premature termination with accelerated degradation and insoluble aggregation (the exon 7 frameshift), and destabilisation or disrupted zinc coordination of an otherwise full-length protein (His107Tyr, p.W123X).

nodes.description: Cytosolic carbonic anhydrase II supplies protons for secretion and bicarbonate for basolateral exit in the proximal tubule, and the same activity in collecting-duct alpha-intercalated cells supports distal proton secretion. Its loss impairs both bicarbonate reclamation and distal acidification, which is why the renal phenotype is most often mixed rather than purely distal. Two observations qualify the cellular picture. First, CA II-deficient patients still respond to intravenous acetazolamide with a rise in urinary pH and bicarbonate excretion, so a separate acetazolamide-sensitive carbonic anhydrase - most plausibly the membrane-bound luminal isoenzyme, which is a different gene product - remains active in their kidneys. Second, in the mouse null the intercalated cell population itself is depleted, so part of the renal defect may be a cell-population phenotype rather than a purely enzymatic one.
nodes.id: Impaired Renal Tubular Proton Secretion and Bicarbonate Reclamation

nodes.description: Calcium deposits accumulate in the brain parenchyma from early childhood, predominantly in basal ganglia and thalami and at the frontal grey-white matter junction, and progress over years. This is the arm that named the disease and the one whose mechanism is least settled: it is not explained by the osteoclast or tubular defects, it does not track neurodevelopmental severity, and no demonstrated intervening step links CA II loss to mineral deposition at these sites. The node is therefore marked HYPOTHETICAL and carries a knowledge-gap discussion rather than a mechanism.

nodes.description: Carbonic anhydrase II catalyses the reversible hydration of CO2 to bicarbonate and a proton, and it does so fast enough to supply transporters working at physiological rates. Its loss removes the rapid intracellular source of both ions simultaneously. This single molecular deficit is the branch point of the disease: the osteoclast loses the protons its ruffled-border pump secretes, the renal tubule loses both the protons it secretes and the bicarbonate it reclaims, and the brain loses the same activity for reasons that remain less well defined.
nodes.id: Loss of Cytosolic Proton and Bicarbonate Supply

nodes.description: Oral bicarbonate or citrate to correct the hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. This is the mainstay for the renal arm and the only arm-directed therapy that is not a transplant. It is worth being precise about its standing: there is no standardised pharmacologic regimen for this disease, and the strongest statement available is an inference from a cohort whose overall phenotype was milder than historical series, whose authors raised the possibility that early bicarbonate treatment was responsible. nodes.description: The osteoclast seals a resorption lacuna against the bone surface and acidifies it to roughly pH 4.5 by pumping protons across the ruffled border with the V-ATPase, with CLCN7 supplying the counter-ion chloride. Carbonic anhydrase II generates those protons in the cytosol. Without it the osteoclast is present, multinucleated and attached but cannot lower the pH of the compartment it has sealed. This is the defining contrast with TCIRG1 and CLCN7 disease, where the pump and the counter-ion conductance themselves fail: the lesion here is upstream of the transport machinery, in the substrate it transports.

evidence.reference_title: A splice junction mutation in intron 2 of the carbonic anhydrase II gene of osteopetrosis patients from Arabic countries.
evidence.snippet: We have analyzed DNAs from members of six unrelated Arabic kindreds and found five to be homozygous and one heterozygous for a novel splice junction (donor site) mutation at the 5' end of intron 2.

evidence.reference_title: A unique mutation underlying carbonic anhydrase II deficiency syndrome in patients of Arab descent.
evidence.snippet: This mutation is found exclusively in patients with an Arabic background and thus may be confined to this ethnic group.

evidence.reference_title: Allogenic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in an Iranian patient with osteopetrosis caused by carbonic anhydrase II deficiency: A case report.
evidence.snippet: Whole-exome sequencing revealed a pathogenic homozygous variant in intron 2 of the carbonic anhydrase 2 gene (CA2) gene (c.232 + 1 G>T).

nodes.description: Homozygous nonsense variant in exon 4 identified in a five-generation Chinese family; minigene and structural work attributed the effect to altered protein modification, impaired zinc binding, and reduced CA2 protein expression.

evidence.reference_title: A novel homozygous nonsense mutation in the CA2 gene (c.368G>A, p.W123X) linked to carbonic anhydrase II deficiency syndrome in a Chinese family.
evidence.snippet: Sequencing and genetic analysis have revealed the homozygous nonsense mutation of CA2 gene (c.368G > A, p.W123X) in the exon 4 of chromosome 8 of the proband

evidence.reference_title: A novel homozygous nonsense mutation in the CA2 gene (c.368G>A, p.W123X) linked to carbonic anhydrase II deficiency syndrome in a Chinese family.
evidence.snippet: Properties and structure of mutated CA2 proteins changed after mutation, especially in change of protein modification and hindrance of zinc ions binding, which may lead to decreased protein expression level of CA2.
